items.abstract: The origin of diagnostic cranial and dental traits of modern East Asians (e.g., shovel‑shaped incisors) has long been interpreted under the Recent African Origin with admixture (RAO) model as a product of late‑arriving exogenous genetic input. Drawing on energy‑information networks and niche dynamics (LSED), this study integrates geological, palaeoanthropological and palaeogenomic evidence to propose the Hydrological Ratchet and pleiotropic amplifier model. Three core findings are established:First, a morphological‑genetic timestamp paradox spanning hundreds of thousands up to nearly one million years is identified. Fully developed shovel‑shaped incisors are present in fossils such as Zhoukoudian Homo erectus (~700 ka) and Hexian hominin (41.2 ka). The incisor morphology of the Lantian hominin (1.63 Ma) is supported by micro‑CT analysis, though its degree of shovelling remains under review. The candidate variant EDAR V370A reached high frequency no earlier than ~30 ka by molecular clock inference (Kamberov et al., 2013), with direct ancient‑DNA evidence anchoring its earliest high‑frequency occurrence at 19 ka (Mao et al., 2021). This million‑year temporal decoupling demonstrates that this variant functions only as a late‑stage amplifier, rather than the originator of this ancient dental phenotype.Second, geological records from the North China Plain and western Shandong deposits show recurrent semi‑grassland, semi‑lacustrine mosaic habitats and cyclic flooding since the Middle Pleistocene. This forms the Hydrological Ratchet, which imposes persistent masticatory mechanical stress. Via developmental canalisation and selection, it repeatedly re‑generates the East Asian morphological groundplan through homoplasy, even without a continuous direct phylogenetic lineage.Third, this morphological groundplan accumulated evolutionary potential within insular refugia shaped by Holocene marine transgression. Coupled with resource capture and power differentiation, it fuelled the state‑formation transition on the western Shandong terraces and gu‑dui mounds, characterised by sea‑salt monopoly, elevated‑platform ritual and class‑based coercion.This work reconstructs an autochthonous evolutionary dynamic for East Asian human morphology, and provides a testable niche‑dynamics framework for the persistent archaeological paradox of morphological continuity amid phylogenetic discontinuity.
